title: Letter 35 — On True Rest
attribution_note: Letter 35 of 46 in the collection Letters Sent — see Letter 1 for provenance.

pairs.en: I received your letter. For the copying of the notebooks I thank you, and I answer both this and the first letter.

To this. In my opinion, there is no better place for you than Lipovka. There a special cell is ready for you, and a solitary place fit for reading, meditation, prayer and the composition of every work of the mind — in a word, according to our science, a place most advantageous. There my nephew also lives; you may from time to time drive away melancholy with him, and by conversation with him gain benefit for yourself as well. For he who teaches is twice taught. And when you wish to go out for a drive, you may also go to Ksizovo with the children for a day. I would, in very truth, live there without going out: so much does that place please me. But men — chiefly my enemies seize occasion to calumniate one living there — for this reason I have shut myself in the monastery, and I shall hardly go anywhere without extreme need. And if for reasons known to you it does not please you to live there, then I have spoken with Nikandr Alexeich, and he wished to make you a hut in the garden at Ksizovo, for your quiet. For the rest, I give counsel, and you act with foresight.

sections.heading: Self-knowledge and the haven of the soul

pairs.en: Answer to the first letter.

1) Knowledge of oneself and of one's heart comes from Holy Scripture and other Christian books. But above all, and more effectually, temptation brings us to the knowledge of ourselves — temptation which comes both from without, through the devil and evil men, and from within, through evil thoughts. Temptation is like the medicine called an emetic, which, taken inwardly, casts out from the stomach juices and food: so temptation shows what is hidden within our heart. And this among other reasons is why God permits temptation to come upon us: that we may know what is hidden in our heart. We often think something of ourselves, but temptation when it comes shows that we are nothing.

2) From this we see that there is no true rest in this world either. We live in the city and among men — scandals and evil people trouble us; we betake ourselves to the wilderness and solitude — there greater and more numerous troubles from Satan and from thoughts. Believe one who has been tried. And so this world, like the sea, always tosses us and everywhere troubles us.

3) If there is any rest in this world, it consists only in a pure conscience and in patience. This is the haven for us who sail the sea of this world. A pure conscience fears not, and therefore the man is at rest. Patience calms and stills the moving and troubled heart, and so sets the man in quiet.

4) Patience cannot be learned without calamities and temptations, for patience is the enduring of evil and of calamities, and not of good and prosperity. Likewise it is impossible to have a good conscience until a man truly repents, and begins to amend his life according to the rule of the word of God.

5) A pure conscience and true patience are inseparable. A pure conscience keeps the word of God, and patience stands against all that opposes God's word, and keeps the conscience, that it be not defiled by transgression, and so that transgression not trouble it.
6) True, continual and untroubled rest is kept for us in eternal life, which is why it is called in Scripture *“rest”* [Hebrews 4:11]. Which I wish both for myself and for you.
